name: SNKV (SnkvDB)
workload: 1M records on Linux; both stores WAL mode, synchronous=NORMAL, 8MB cache, 4KB pages, SQLite uses a WITHOUT ROWID table; sequential writes, random reads, sequential scan, random updates/deletes, mixed workload.
claimed_speedup: 1.64x-2x faster across operations: sequential writes 232K vs 142K ops/s, random reads 160K vs 90K ops/s, sequential scan 2.89M vs 1.56M ops/s, random updates/deletes ~1.9-2x, mixed workload 62K vs 34K ops/s.
tradeoffs: C API talks directly to SQLite's B-tree/pager/WAL layer with no SQL parser or query planner; loses schema-layer tooling (sqlite3 CLI) though it is compatible with SQLite page/WAL-level tools like LiteFS; optional encryption and HNSW vector index add build complexity.
caveats: Numbers come from the project's own test suite (tests/test_benchmark.c); no CPU model or compiler flags stated. Separate comparison repos hash-anu/lmdb-benchmark and hash-anu/rocksdb-benchmark exist but contain only benchmark source code with no published result numbers, so they could not be used as evidence here.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): gh search repos "faster than sqlite"; HN Algolia "single file database faster than sqlite"

name: HyperLevelDB
workload: InfluxDB storage-engine shootout: 100 million key-value pairs across 500,000 series columns, 24-byte (3-int) keys, protobuf-serialized values, batches of 1,000 writes; write N, query N, delete N/2, compact, query remaining N/2, write N/2 more.
claimed_speedup: Identified as the fastest engine for writes among LevelDB/RocksDB/HyperLevelDB/LMDB at 100M-value scale; RocksDB won reads/deletes and LevelDB was most disk-efficient in the same test (no exact numeric ratio is given on the page).
hardware: DigitalOcean droplet: 4GB RAM, 2 CPU cores, 60GB SSD (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Fork of LevelDB by the now-defunct HyperDex team, adds multi-threaded compaction; abandoned since 2016 so it lacks a decade of LevelDB/RocksDB fixes.
caveats: 2014 benchmark on modest hardware; the author explicitly states settings were not tuned per engine ('we haven't had the time to tune any settings...'); only categorical per-metric winners are stated, no exact throughput numbers, so no numeric speedup is claimed here.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia "leveldb vs lmdb vs rocksdb benchmark" -> InfluxData blog post

name: Badger (BadgerDB)
workload: populate + random-read benchmark: 250M keys with 128-byte values for the read test, and 75M keys with 1KB values for the population/write-time test; Badger's WiscKey-style value log vs RocksDB SSTables.
claimed_speedup: Random reads: Badger is 3.67x faster (32361 ns/op vs 118982 ns/op for RocksDB). Population of 75M x 1KB records: 17m10s (Badger) vs 78m8s (RocksDB), about 4.6x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.8; RocksDB v5.1.4 built via `make shared_lib` with USE_RTTI=1
hardware: Amazon EC2 i3.large dedicated instance: 2 cores, 16GB RAM, 450GB local NVMe SSD (fio measured ~93K random-read IOPS at 4K block size)
stars_or_usage: 15.8k stars; used by IPFS, Usenet Express, Decred, Insolar, IoTex, 194+ dependent Go packages
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no Cgo; separates keys from values (WiscKey design) so full-value iteration is much slower than RocksDB's (see companion BENCH-lmdb-bolt.md iterate-with-values numbers); higher resident memory during population (14GB+ RSS) than RocksDB in this test.
caveats: Benchmark was run in 2017 against RocksDB v5.1.4, which is old; the badger-bench repo itself has been archived since 2022 with no newer published re-run found.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia "badger rocksdb" -> blog.dgraph.io post -> dgraph-io/badger-bench repo (BENCH-rocks.txt)

name: CacheAdvance
workload: Appending log messages (a Lorum Ipsum message set) to an on-disk cache file, single-message and batch append, measured with XCTest `measure {}` performance tests against an equivalent SQLite-backed cache.
claimed_speedup: "CacheAdvance persists log events 30x faster than SQLite" (README headline claim).
tradeoffs: No in-memory buffer, every append is a synchronous disk write; not thread-safe (single serial queue only); the SQLite comparison test is disabled on Linux (Apple platforms only).
caveats: The 30x figure is a first-party README claim; the XCTest benchmark code is public but the README does not state CPU model, Xcode/Swift version, or dataset size alongside the number.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): gh search repos "faster than sqlite"

name: DBX
workload: 10,000-record in-memory INSERT benchmark comparing DBX's Tier-1 (BTreeMap, 'Fast-Path' v0.2.0) against SQLite.
claimed_speedup: Memory INSERT 1.16x faster than SQLite (25ms vs 29ms for the stated run).
tradeoffs: 0.2.0-beta software; the README's larger '29x' and '4.5x GPU' claims are versus 'traditional B-Tree engines' and CUDA baselines, not versus SQLite directly, so only the 1.16x figure is a real SQLite comparison.
caveats: Very small, very new project (4 stars, created Feb 2026); no hardware or compiler stated; only a 10,000-record sample; marketing-heavy README with an unfilled Ko-fi placeholder link. GitHub's license detector reports 'NOASSERTION' even though the LICENSE file text is standard MIT (verified by reading it directly). Treat with low confidence.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): gh search repos "faster than sqlite"

name: ForestDB
workload: Mobile-side test on a Google Nexus 5: 1M documents loaded, key length 8-32 bytes, value size 256 bytes; random read of 80K records, random update of 80K records (batch size 1-20), and a mixed read+update workload; ForestDB vs a single two-column SQLite table (WAL mode).
claimed_speedup: Reads up to 8x faster than SQLite; writes up to 2.3x faster than SQLite (at larger batch sizes); mixed workload up to 7x faster than SQLite.
compiler_and_flags: SQLite 3.7.11 on Android KitKat 4.4.2 (native compiler/flags not stated)
hardware: Google Nexus 5, Qualcomm Snapdragon 800 MSM8974 (quad-core, 2260MHz, Krait 400), 2GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; formerly the storage engine of Couchbase Server / Couchbase Lite
tradeoffs: The same page also compares ForestDB server-side against LevelDB v1.15 and RocksDB v3.1 on an Intel Xeon E5-2620 box: ForestDB showed much lower write amplification (7x-20x vs RocksDB's 31x-35x and LevelDB's 166x-387x), but those server-side throughput numbers are only shown as bar-chart images, not text, so they are not quoted as a numeric claim here.
caveats: This analysis section is HTML-commented-out on the live wiki page (the rendered page only shows 'new benchmark results and analysis will be available soon'); the numbers above were recovered from the page's raw Markdown source. Results date from 2014, are first-party (Couchbase's own team), and the repo's own README says the 'master' branch is unsupported/community-only.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia "forestdb" -> couchbaselabs/forestdb README -> ForestDB-Benchmark wiki -> forestdb wiki Performance-Results page

name: LUDA
workload: YCSB cloud benchmark, 16-byte keys, value sizes 128B-1KB, YCSB-A workload (0.5/0.5 update-read ratio); 10 million key-value pairs loaded, plus a larger 0.1-billion-pair (50GB) run; GPU-accelerated compaction vs stock LevelDB and RocksDB.
claimed_speedup: Up to 2x higher throughput and 2x data processing speed than LevelDB and RocksDB, with more stable 99th-percentile latencies.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 10.1; built on LevelDB v1.22 (~1K LOC modified, +2.7K LOC CUDA) compared against RocksDB v6.4.6
hardware: Supermicro X10DAI, Intel Xeon E5-1620 v4 (4-core/8-thread), 64GB DRAM, one NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti GPU, one 280GB Intel Optane 900p SSD; Ubuntu 16.04, kernel 4.15
tradeoffs: Requires a discrete NVIDIA GPU and CUDA; only bloom-filter/compaction sorting is GPU-accelerated, snappy compression is not yet supported; benefits are largest when the host CPU is otherwise busy.
caveats: The paper states 'we are ready to open source it' but only gives a footnote link to an anonymized double-blind-review placeholder (github.com/anonymous); no real public repository was found, so has_code=false and repo_url is null. Full hardware/software methodology is otherwise well documented, which is why this is not tier D.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): arXiv API search "embedded key value store benchmark" -> LUDA: Boost LSM Key Value Store Compactions with GPUs (arXiv:2004.03054)
